title: Same Brand, Different Recipe: Why India's Maggi, Fanta, and KitKat Have More Sugar and Less Cocoa Than UK Versions
excerpt: A Reuters investigation reveals how global food giants resist front-of-pack warning labels in India while voluntarily adding them in Europe, and how industry lobbying derailed FSSAI's push for color-coded warnings.
body:
• A can of Fanta sold in India contains roughly three times the sugar of the same brand sold in the UK — 13.7g per 100ml versus 4.5g — plus an artificial dye that requires a health warning in Europe.
  • All Maggi noodle variants sold in India use palm oil, while many UK versions use pricier sunflower oil. Maggi packets made in India and exported to Britain carry a red front-of-pack salt warning that the same product lacks domestically.
  • India's KitKat contains 4.5% cocoa solids compared to at least 22% in Australia's version.
  • FSSAI abandoned its push for color-coded front-of-pack warning labels after a March 2026 meeting with industry executives, a decision the Supreme Court is now scrutinizing.

A 330ml can of Fanta Orange bought in London contains about 63 calories. The same brand sold in India packs roughly 185 calories — three times the sugar, plus an artificial coloring agent that European rules require to carry a child-health warning. The Indian can notes the dye only in small print on the back.

This is not a one-off. A Reuters investigation published on August 25 lays out in detail how multinational food companies sell meaningfully different products in India compared to what they offer in Europe and Australia — and how industry lobbying has so far blocked India from requiring the kind of clear, front-of-pack warnings that would make those differences visible at a glance.

The Product-by-Product Gap

The numbers tell a stark story. Coca-Cola India's published nutritional data lists Fanta at 13.7g of sugar per 100ml, against 4.5g per 100ml in the UK version. The Indian formulation also includes Colour 110 (Sunset Yellow FCF, or E110), one of the "Southampton Six" synthetic dyes that EU and UK rules require to carry the warning: "may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children." India has no such requirement.

Nestlé's Maggi instant noodles tell a similar story. Every variant sold in India is made with palm oil. Many versions sold in Britain — including packets manufactured in India — use sunflower oil, which is lower in saturated fat. Those same India-made packets carry a red front-of-pack label warning of high salt content when they reach UK shelves. Inside India, no such warning appears.

"It is the frustration of feeling cheated."

— Revant Himatsingka, social media activist known as Food Pharmer

Indian KitKats contain 4.5% cocoa solids, while the Australian version's milk chocolate has at least 22% cocoa — meaning the Indian bar substitutes the rest with proportionally more sugar and fat.

How Industry Lobbying Derailed Warning Labels

India's FSSAI had been working on mandatory front-of-pack warnings since 2017, floating proposals for color-coded labels and star ratings. But at a March 2026 meeting with industry executives — details of which Reuters reported for the first time — the regulator backed off.

Coca-Cola India executive Mili Bhattacharya told FSSAI it was "very simplistic" to believe warning labels would change consumer behavior. Deepak Jolly of the Indian Food & Beverage Association said packaging would be "awash in red" if color-coded labels were adopted — since industry estimates suggest 80% of India's over $100 billion packaged food market could be classified as high in fat, sugar, or salt.

The irony is hard to miss. Coca-Cola has voluntarily added traffic-light-style labels to its drinks in some two dozen European markets. Nestlé has used interpretive labels in Britain since 2013. Neither company adopted similar practices in India. Both declined to comment for the Reuters report.

The Supreme Court Steps In

India's Supreme Court is now scrutinizing FSSAI's decision. After the regulator told the court in August that matching international labelling standards was "difficult," the judges responded: "the world should know that India is very much concerned about the overall health of its citizens."

The court had already directed regulators in February to consider introducing warning labels, suggesting they examine Israel's red-and-green system. Health activists have petitioned for stronger labels, pointing to a Lancet study projecting that 450 million Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050.

Signs of Slow Change

Consumer awareness is pushing some companies to adapt. Nestlé in 2024 began selling sugar-free Cerelac baby food in India after years of selling only the sugar-containing version — a formulation gap flagged by activists. FSSAI in July ordered PepsiCo to drop the "energy drink" label from its Sting caffeine drink within 90 days.

For Indian consumers, the takeaway is straightforward: a familiar global brand name does not guarantee the same formulation you would get abroad. Until front-of-pack warnings arrive, the back-of-pack nutrition table remains the only reliable check — and most shoppers never turn the packet over.
nri_angle: NRIs who regularly buy Indian brands like Maggi in ethnic grocery stores abroad are often consuming different formulations than what the same brand sells in the UK or US, raising questions about what version they are actually getting.
